challenges.name: concurrent-refresh-evidence
challenges.title: Concurrent Refresh & Token Replay: read the evidence
challenges.description: A learner's phone resumed, refreshed twice with the same token 40 ms apart, got two 200 responses, and 15 minutes later was flagged as a replay and signed out on every device. Six statements on one evidence pack - the API log (A), the refresh code (B), the PostgreSQL statement log (C) and the rows of the family (D) - take you from the evidence to a hypothesis, past two wrong explanations, to the fix and its test.

questions.question:
Evidence B - AuthService.refresh, as shipped:
async refresh(token: string, deviceId: string): Promise<RefreshResult> {
  const row = await this.tokens.findByHash(sha256(token));    // SELECT * FROM refresh_tokens WHERE token_hash = $1
  if (!row || row.revokedAt) throw new UnauthorizedException();
  if (this.clock.now() >= row.expiresAt) throw new UnauthorizedException();
  if (row.usedAt) return this.handleReuse(row, deviceId);      // replay detection (lesson 3.1)

  await this.tokens.retireLiveTokens(row.familyId);           // UPDATE ... SET used_at = now() WHERE family_id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL
  const next = await this.tokens.issue(row);                  // INSERT INTO refresh_tokens ...
  await this.tokens.recordSuccessor(row.id, next);            // UPDATE ... SET replaced_by = $2 WHERE id = $1
  return { status: "rotated", token: next.token };
}

Evidence C - PostgreSQL statement log, request id in brackets:
09:14:03.121 [7f1a] SELECT * FROM refresh_tokens WHERE token_hash = $1                 -> r_901, used_at NULL
09:14:03.162 [7f1b] SELECT * FROM refresh_tokens WHERE token_hash = $1                 -> r_901, used_at NULL
09:14:03.178 [7f1a] UPDATE refresh_tokens SET used_at = now()
                    WHERE family_id = 'f_77' AND used_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL -> UPDATE 1
09:14:03.183 [7f1a] INSERT INTO refresh_tokens (id, family_id, ...) VALUES ('r_902', 'f_77', ...)
09:14:03.186 [7f1a] UPDATE refresh_tokens SET replaced_by = 'r_902' WHERE id = 'r_901'
09:14:03.205 [7f1b] UPDATE refresh_tokens SET used_at = now()
                    WHERE family_id = 'f_77' AND used_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL -> UPDATE 1
09:14:03.209 [7f1b] INSERT INTO refresh_tokens (id, family_id, ...) VALUES ('r_903', 'f_77', ...)
09:14:03.212 [7f1b] UPDATE refresh_tokens SET replaced_by = 'r_903' WHERE id = 'r_901'

Statement: "Both requests read r_901 with used_at NULL before either of them wrote to it, so the `if (row.usedAt)` check in the code passed for both."
questions.explanation: True. C shows 7f1a's SELECT at .121 and 7f1b's SELECT at .162, and the first write (7f1a's UPDATE) only at .178. Each request checked its own copy of the row in application code, and both copies said used_at NULL. Nothing in the database connected the check to the later write, so the check could not stop the second request. This is the classic check-then-act race; the misconception is that a check in code protects a write that happens several awaits later.

Evidence D - family f_77 after the incident (SELECT id, device_id, used_at, revoked_at, replaced_by ...):

Statement: "Request 7f1b's family-wide UPDATE marked r_902 as used, because at 09:14:03.205 r_902 was the only row of f_77 with used_at NULL; the phone kept r_902 because response 7f1a was sent last, so its next refresh presented a token that was already marked used."
questions.explanation: True. This hypothesis explains every piece of evidence. In C, 7f1a inserted r_902 at .183; at .205 7f1b ran the same "retire the live token" UPDATE for the whole family, and the only live row by then was r_902 (D shows r_902 used at .205 although no request ever presented it then). In A, 7f1a took 212 ms and 7f1b 131 ms, so 7f1a's response (and its Set-Cookie with r_902) arrived after 7f1b's and overwrote it on the phone. Fifteen minutes later the phone presented r_902, which was used and outside any grace window, so the replay detection did exactly what it was built to do.

Statement: "The 09:29 alarm was a real theft: r_902 was used at 09:14:03.205 by someone other than the phone, so signing the learner out everywhere was the right outcome."
questions.explanation: False. The API log shows only two requests in that second, both from phone-8812 and both presenting r_901; nobody presented r_902 until the phone itself did at 09:29:05. The used_at on r_902 at .205 is the timestamp of 7f1b's family-wide UPDATE in C, not of a refresh. A replay alarm is a strong signal, but it is evidence to check, not a verdict: here every request came from the same device and the timeline explains the used_at without a second party. The misconception is to trust the alarm's label instead of the timeline that produced it.

Statement: "Clock skew explains the race: 40 ms is too long for two requests to overlap, so 7f1b must have started after 7f1a committed, and only skewed clocks on api-1 and api-2 make their statements look interleaved."
questions.explanation: False. The timestamps in C come from one clock, the database server's, so skew between api-1 and api-2 cannot reorder them, and they show 7f1b's SELECT (.162) before 7f1a's first write (.178). 40 ms is long compared with a single statement but short compared with the handler: 7f1a needed 57 ms between its read and its write (a network round trip per await). Any second request that reads inside that gap sees the old row. The misconception is that races need requests to arrive at the same millisecond; they only need to overlap the read-to-write gap.

Statement: "Changing the UPDATE to `WHERE id = $1` (r_901 only) is enough: each request then retires only the row it read, and both requests can safely answer 200."
questions.explanation: False. With `WHERE id = $1` 7f1b would no longer touch r_902, so this particular sign-out would not happen, but both requests would still pass the check and both would insert a successor: two live tokens, r_902 and r_903, in one family. That fork is the real danger: a stolen copy of r_901 raced alongside the phone would get its own live branch, and replay detection would never see a reuse. The write itself must be the check - `UPDATE ... SET used_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL RETURNING *` - and the code must act on whether it got a row: the winner rotates, the loser answers with the winner's successor (grace) or asks the client to retry.

Statement: "A test that pauses request A right after its SELECT, lets request B run its SELECT, and then runs both to the end fails on the shipped code (two rotated results with different tokens) and passes after the fix (one rotated, one grace with the same token)."
questions.explanation: True. The test forces the exact interleaving from C instead of hoping the timing happens: both reads before any write. On the shipped code both requests rotate and the family forks; after the compare-and-swap fix only one UPDATE returns a row, and the loser, from the same device inside the window, gets the winner's successor. A test that fires two real requests and hopes they overlap passes or fails depending on timing, which is why the scheduler pauses at a named statement: the same interleaving every run.

challenges.name: concurrent-refresh-compare-and-swap
challenges.title: Concurrent Refresh
challenges.description:
When the CodeDev phone app resumes, two requests can call POST /auth/refresh with the same refresh token 40 ms apart. In production both answered 200 with two different tokens, and on the next refresh the phone was flagged as a replay and the learner was signed out on every device. Fix refresh() so that, however the statements of concurrent requests interleave, exactly one request rotates the token.

Required results: the winner gets {status:"rotated", token}; a request that lost the race, comes from the row's device and is less than GRACE_MS = 10000 ms after the row's usedAt gets the winner's successor {status:"grace", token} and nothing new is issued; if the winner has not recorded its successor yet (replacedBy still null) the loser gets {status:"retry"} (the API answers 409 and the client tries again 100 ms later), with no revocation and no event. A reuse from another device, after the window, or after the successor was used is still a replay: revoke the family, record one refresh_token_reuse event and return {status:"replay_detected"}. Invalid, revoked and expired tokens keep their answers, and a winner whose family was revoked meanwhile (issue returns null) answers "revoked". Issue a successor only for the request that won.

Each Db method is one atomic SQL statement, listed in the store; markUsed is UPDATE refresh_tokens SET used_at = $2 WHERE id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL RETURNING *. The test runner is a deterministic scheduler: a step {op:"concurrent", requests:[{id, token, device, at}], schedule:[["A","findByHash"], ["B","findByHash"], ["A","end"], ...]} runs request A until it completes its next findByHash statement, then B, and so on; unfinished requests then run to the end in order. Tokens are labels ("t2" = the token of row r2), "@A" (the token last returned to request A) or literal strings. Output: one line per request ("B refresh t1 phone @900040: grace t2"), then the security events and every row ("r1 f1 phone used=900000 revoked=- next=r2"); with "quiet": true, a summary.
hints: Run the first public test on the starter and read the rows at the end. Between request A reading the row and writing to it, what did request B see, and which row did B's write change?

Look at the rotation step in refresh(): the check `row.usedAt !== null` uses a copy read earlier, and retireLiveTokens updates whatever is live in the family when it runs. The store has a statement whose result tells you whether you were the one who changed used_at. Then look at what handleReuse does when the successor is not recorded yet.

A similar race on different data: two requests redeem the same one-time voucher. `SELECT used FROM vouchers WHERE code = $1` then `UPDATE vouchers SET used = true WHERE code = $1` lets both pass. `UPDATE vouchers SET used = true WHERE code = $1 AND used = false RETURNING id` returns a row to exactly one of them; the other reads the voucher again and answers from what the winner left (here: the order it created, or 'try again' if the order is not saved yet).
